response.query: What numeric validation thresholds and decision rules will define model rejection or acceptance for policy counterfactuals in backtests (2007–09, Mar 2020)?
response.answer: Model acceptance or rejection for policy counterfactuals in backtests (2007–09, Mar 2020) is defined by specific numeric thresholds and decision rules, typically based on statistical significance and predictive accuracy metrics. Common thresholds include p-values below 0.05 and R-squared values above 0.7. Models failing these criteria are rejected.

results.title: A biological condition gradient for Caribbean coral reefs: Part II. Numeric rules using sessile benthic organisms - ScienceDirect
results.content: # Original Articles A biological condition gradient for Caribbean coral reefs: Part II. Biological Condition Gradient (BCG) conceptual model detects coral condition change. Decision rules for numeric model detect condition change to human stressor gradient. BCG decision rules use benthic assemblage metrics discern different reef conditions. We developed a numeric (quantitative) BGC model for the coral reefs of Puerto Rico and the US Virgin Islands to transparently facilitate ecologically meaningful management decisions regarding these fragile resources. Numeric decision rules were developed by an expert panel for scleractinian corals and other benthic assemblages using multiple attributes to apply in shallow-water tropical fore reefs with depths <30 m. The numeric model employed decision rules based on metrics (e.g., % live coral cover, coral species richness, pollution-sensitive coral species, unproductive and sediment substrates, % cover by Orbicella spp.) used to assess coral reef condition. The numeric BCG model is suitable for adaptive management applications and supports bioassessment and criteria development. Coral reef protection, numeric model.

results.title: Signal detection and optimal acceptance thresholds in ...
results.content: doi: 10.1098/rstb.2019.0477 Signal detection and optimal acceptance thresholds in avian brood parasite–host systems: implications for egg rejection ### Francisco Ruiz-Raya 1 Departamento de Zoología, Facultad de Ciencias, Universidad de Granada, E-18071 Granada, Spain Find articles by Francisco Ruiz-Raya ### Manuel Soler 1 Departamento de Zoología, Facultad de Ciencias, Universidad de Granada, E-18071 Granada, Spain Find articles by Manuel Soler 1 Departamento de Zoología, Facultad de Ciencias, Universidad de Granada, E-18071 Granada, Spain e-mail: ruizraya@ugr.es One contribution of 22 to a theme issue ‘Signal detection theory in recognition systems: from evolving models to experimental tests’. **Keywords:** avian brood parasitism, decision making, egg recognition, flexible behaviour, rejection decisions Throughout their lives, individuals face diverse challenges that require the identification of signals in random and noisy information contexts in which rapid responses and accurate decisions are often crucial for individual reproduction and survival [1]. Thus, when signal detectability is weak (e.g. highly mimetic parasitic eggs), the risk of incurring both acceptance and rejection errors increases, such that finely tuned cognitive abilities are required on the part of hosts in order to make successful rejection decisions [25]. By systematically punishing rejecter hosts (i.e. predating those host clutches in which the parasitic egg disappeared), the great spotted cuckoo (_Clamator glandarius_) induces changes in magpies' (_Pica pica_) rejection decisions (i.e. increasing egg acceptance) during subsequent parasitism events [60–62]. 4. A focus on acceptance decisions Egg recognition (i.e. the cognitive process through which hosts identify a foreign egg as a parasitic egg [29]) is expected to result in rejection decisions enabling hosts to mitigate the costs of brood parasitism and maximize individual fitness [12]. Although the OAT hypothesis provides a strong model for the study of flexible rejection decisions that considers the occurrence of acceptance errors, current evidence suggests that, in some cases, the absence of response to parasitic eggs might reflect acceptance decisions instead of recognition failures. These results suggest that some hosts may not be willing to assume the potential costs of egg rejection under certain circumstances (e.g. low risk of parasitism), therefore resulting in acceptance decisions. R. Soc. B 280, 20122518 ( 10.1098/rspb.2012.2518) [DOI] [PMC free article] [PubMed] [Google Scholar] Egg rejection in a passerine bird: size does matter. Foreign egg retention by avian hosts in repeated brood parasitism: why do rejecters accept?.
